new_findings_today.title: The cinematic destination-page template became the default for EVERY known destination on 2026-10-04 -- the long-tracked Hindi-H1 gap (NEW-2026-07-09-001) and decorative-coordinate bug (NEW-2026-06-06-003) are now effectively universal (533/533), not scoped to ~70% of the catalog
new_findings_today.detail: This run's Section K check hit betla, the SKILL.md's long-standing designated 'known non-cinematic destination' used every week specifically to keep Leaflet-template coverage from being lost to random sampling (per NEW-2026-08-24-002). betla no longer renders the Leaflet template: 0 .leaflet-container elements, 0 occurrences of the string 'leaflet' anywhere in its page HTML, and it now shows the same atlas SVG (viewBox 0 0 1000 1100) as every cinematic destination. A second spot-check (arambol, Goa, also DB content_tier='B') confirmed the same. Reading the source directly (apps/web/src/lib/cinematic-destinations.ts) explains why: 'Cinematic template gate. Since 2026-10-04 EVERY known destination renders via DestinationDetailCinematic by default... Until then this was a hand-kept allowlist frozen at 505 slugs (2026-05-16); the 28 destinations added later silently kept the old DestinationDetail page for months (founder spotted betla).' The file's own LEGACY_DESTINATIONS escape-hatch set is empty, and known-destination-slugs.json has exactly 533 entries matching destinations_total_db -- so isCinematicDestination() returns true for all 533 destinations with no exceptions. Git commit 8574f057 ('feat(destination): new design is the default for every destination; backfill the 28 left behind') made this change. The qa/cinematic-readiness.md tracker's 'A+HS-B=377 cinematic-eligible' figure is a CONTENT-completeness gate (widget data thresholds for gems/eats/stays), not a template-selection gate -- it no longer describes which destinations get the cinematic page shell, only which ones have enough data to fill every section of it. Confirmed directly in DB: betla and arambol are both content_tier='B' (not in the 377 'eligible' count) yet both render the cinematic template live. Downstream consequence: NEW-2026-07-09-001 (destination H1 renders in English on /hi) and NEW-2026-06-06-003 (decorative '23.5' coordinate string on every cinematic page) were both scoped in every prior week's report as affecting '~377/533 (71%) of the catalog, the cinematic template'. That scoping is now out of date -- both bugs are very likely present on all 533 destination pages, since all 533 now use the cinematic template. This was not independently re-verified on all 533 pages this run (time-boxed to the two spot-checked destinations, tawang and betla), but the code-level evidence (empty LEGACY_DESTINATIONS, 533/533 known-slugs match) is unambiguous that the template itself is universal.
new_findings_today.evidence: javascript_tool on live betla page: leaflet_count=0, leaflet_string_count=0, atlas_svg=true. Same on arambol. apps/web/src/lib/cinematic-destinations.ts source read via device_bash: LEGACY_DESTINATIONS is an empty Set; comment states 'Since 2026-10-04 EVERY known destination renders via DestinationDetailCinematic by default'. git log -- apps/web/src/lib/cinematic-destinations.ts shows commit 8574f057 'new design is the default for every destination; backfill the 28 left behind'. DB: SELECT content_tier FROM destinations WHERE id IN ('betla','arambol') -> both 'B'. known-destination-slugs.json slug count = 533 = destinations_total_db.
new_findings_today.recommendation: Three separate actions: (1) Ashish/engineering -- given the Hindi-H1 gap (NEW-2026-07-09-001) likely now affects 100% of destinations instead of ~70%, consider re-prioritizing it; it was already flagged as the most visible open item in last week's business report at 70% scope. (2) SKILL.md maintenance -- the Section K 'map-type note' describing a destination-page dual-template (atlas vs Leaflet) is now stale; update it to state the Leaflet destination-page template was fully retired 2026-10-04 and only /explore and /treks still use real Leaflet. The designated 'known non-cinematic destination' probe target (betla) should be retired or replaced with a note that no such destination exists anymore. (3) QA follow-up -- next run (or a one-off this week if convenient) should sample a few more destinations across different content_tier values (A/HS-B/B) to directly confirm the H1-English gap is indeed present on all of them, not just the two checked here, before fully closing the re-scoping loop.

new_findings_today.title: Destination month sub-route URL scheme is now NAMED months (/destination/<slug>/december), not numeric (/destination/<slug>/12) -- a probe-methodology note, not a site defect
new_findings_today.detail: This run's first pass at the Section D month-sub-route SEO check used /en/destination/vedanthangal/12 (numeric), which 404'd -- initially looked like a possible regression. Checking the live destination page's own month-navigation links showed they are all named (e.g. href="/en/destination/tawang/december"), and every numeric path (1 through 12) 404s for every destination tested (tawang, vedanthangal, hanle). Re-running the check against the correct named-month URL (/en/destination/vedanthangal/december) returned 200 with a correct, non-stuttering title ('Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary in December: 21–28°C | NakshIQ'), canonical, all three hreflang tags, and og:image all present. This mirrors last week's hreflang case-sensitivity gotcha (NEW-2026-10-05-003) -- a probe-methodology issue that could have been misreported as a site regression if not double-checked against the live page's own markup first.
new_findings_today.evidence: curl /en/destination/tawang/12, /1, /6, /10, /11 -- all 404. grep of tawang's rendered HTML for href="/en/destination/tawang/<month-name>" -- all 12 named months present and linked. curl /en/destination/vedanthangal/december -> 200, title/canonical/hreflang/og:image all correct.
new_findings_today.recommendation: If Section A's garbage-month-sub-route probes are ever changed to use specific numeric values as 'known-good' controls (they currently use clearly-invalid values like 999/13/00, which still correctly 404 either way), update them to use a named-month value instead so a future run doesn't misread the named-month migration as a routing regression.

business_summary.headline: The site is healthy and fast this week, with no broken pages, no server errors, and every safety-critical emergency number still in place across all 533 destinations. The main story this week isn't something that broke -- it's something this check discovered mid-run: a feature rollout that finished site-wide on October 4th turned out to be bigger than last week's report understood. The newer, more polished destination-page design (the one most of the catalog had already switched to) is now actually used on every single destination page, not most of them. That's good news on its own -- a cleaner, more consistent experience everywhere -- but it also means a cosmetic issue we've been tracking for weeks (Hindi destination pages showing their main heading in English) likely now touches the whole catalog instead of about 70% of it, since the page design that carries that issue is no longer the exception, it's the rule. Nothing about this is a new problem introduced this week; it's an existing, known, cosmetic issue whose true size this check is only now correctly measuring. Two smaller, routine items also came up: a connection issue with one of our monitoring tools continued for a second week, and a small number of new backend access-control items appeared alongside a database update, all low-priority and expected as the product keeps evolving.
traffic_lights: Every page we checked loaded correctly -- 10/10 sampled destinations, all core sections (trip planner, explore, emergency info, blog, treks, and more), both languages. Two pages loaded a bit slower than usual on their first (cold) load, which is expected and not a problem.
All 533 destinations in the catalog have verified emergency numbers on file. The 10 we sampled in detail averaged about 7.6 working phone numbers each, every one above our minimum safety threshold.

All 12 pages we checked have correct titles, correct canonical links, correct language-alternate links, and social-preview images. One of our own checks briefly used an outdated web-address format for a specific kind of page before we caught and corrected it -- the site itself was never at fault, see 'About this report'.
Design consistency across the destination catalog

NEW THIS WEEK (confirmed, not newly shipped): the newer, more polished destination-page design -- which most of the site had already moved to -- is now confirmed live on literally every one of the 533 destination pages, not just the roughly 70% we understood it to cover as of last week. This is a positive consistency win: visitors now get the same modern page design wherever they go on the site.

Hindi pages load correctly with correct Hindi titles everywhere. On destination pages specifically, the big on-page headline still shows in English instead of Hindi, even though everything else on the page -- including the browser tab title -- is correctly in Hindi. This is the same known issue as last week, but this week's check revealed it almost certainly now affects every destination page rather than about 70% of them, because of the design-consistency item above. Nothing changed about the bug itself this week; we just now understand its true size.

Two internal automations that run independently of the main website (a newsletter-delivery checker and the 'where to stay' recommendation refresher) each still have an open question from prior weeks that wasn't re-investigated this run, to keep this week's check efficient. Neither affects anything a visitor sees today.
Still running weekly instead of the originally-intended daily cadence -- unchanged from last week, still a configuration decision for Ashish, not a website problem.

Couldn't check this for the second week running -- the tool we use to look at server error logs still isn't connecting. Not an indication of a site problem, just a continuing gap in this week's check.
Sends and engagement both grew again this week (sends up from 52 to 62, engagement events up from 155 to 190); subscriber count held steady.

A small number of new low-priority backend items appeared this week -- two routine database backup snapshots and one new internal function that isn't yet locked down to only the people who should use it. None of this is visible to visitors or affects how the site behaves; it's the kind of routine hardening checklist item that accumulates naturally as the product keeps shipping new features.
whats_changed: DISCOVERED this week (not newly shipped this week -- it happened October 4th and this check is the first to accurately report its true scope): the newer destination-page design is now used on all 533 destinations, not about 70% as previously understood. This is a positive consistency change for visitors, but it also means the Hindi-headline cosmetic issue (see below) almost certainly now has a much wider reach than previously reported.

The Hindi-headline-shows-in-English issue is unchanged in nature but now understood to affect the whole catalog rather than most of it -- this is a correction to our understanding of an existing issue's size, not a new defect.
Newsletter sends and engagement both grew again this week, continuing steady organic growth.
A small website update went out with one new database change and a couple of routine backend housekeeping items -- nothing visitors would notice.
risks: The Hindi-headline issue on destination pages is now understood to likely affect all 533 destinations rather than about 70% of them -- it remains cosmetic (the rest of each page, including the browser tab title, is correctly in Hindi), but this raises its visibility and makes it a stronger candidate for a near-term fix given how many more pages it now touches.

This week's discovery came from a routine spot-check noticing something unexpected, not from a planned full audit -- only 3 of 533 destination pages were directly re-checked live this week to confirm the new understanding. The next check should broaden that sample to build more confidence before treating the 100%-scope conclusion as fully settled.
This automated check is still running weekly instead of daily -- worth deciding whether that's intentional going forward.

The server-error-log monitoring tool has now failed to connect for two weeks running, which is itself worth a look even though it hasn't caused any visible site issue -- it just means two weeks with no visibility into that one category of behind-the-scenes errors.
bottom_line: No urgent action needed -- the site is healthy, fast, and safety-critical information (emergency contacts) remains complete everywhere.

The most useful thing to come out of this week's check is a corrected understanding of how far the Hindi-headline issue reaches -- worth factoring into any decision about when to schedule a fix, since it likely now affects the entire destination catalog rather than most of it.
Worth a quick decision on the automated check's schedule (weekly vs. daily) when convenient -- this has been flagged for a few weeks now.
